q: What is the zero value of an int, a string and a bool?
code:
var i int
var s string
var b bool
explain: Every Go variable starts at a useful zero value — no undefined, no null surprises. Slices, maps and funcs start as nil.

q: What does := do, and where is it forbidden?
explain: := is short declaration. It declares a new variable and infers the type. You cannot use it at package level — use var there.

q: How many loop keywords does Go have?
explain: Go has no while or until. Plain for, condition-only for (while-style), for-range, and infinite for {} all use the same keyword.

q: What do i and v hold here?
explain: range yields index + a COPY. Mutating v does not touch the slice. Use for i := range s if you only need indexes.

q: What numbers do A, B, C get?
explain: Think of iota as a line counter that starts at 0: each line in the const block bumps it by one, and a blank expression repeats the line above. So A=0, B=1, C=2. It resets to 0 in every new const block — the classic enum trick.

q: Why does this compile even though x is unused?
explain: Go refuses to compile unused imports/variables. Assigning to _ tells the compiler “I am discarding this on purpose” — essential for multi-return functions.

q: Println vs Printf — which formats verbs like %d?
explain: Printf interprets %d %s %v. Println just prints args with spaces and a trailing newline. Mixing them up is a classic rookie bug.

q: Do you need break in a Go switch?
explain: Go cases do NOT fall through by default (the opposite of C). Multiple matches go comma-separated. Use fallthrough explicitly if you really want it.

q: What length and capacity does this slice have?
explain: make(type, len, cap) pre-allocates. Length is what you can index today; capacity is room before append must reallocate.

q: What happens to a after append?
explain: append returns a NEW slice header. It may reuse the backing array, so always use the return value: a = append(a, x). Never ignore it.

q: What prints here — and why is it sneaky?
explain: A slice is just a window onto a shared backing array, and slicing opens a second window onto the SAME array — no copying happens. Writes through b are visible through a. Rule: if you need independence, copy explicitly with copy() or append([]T{}, s...).

q: How do you safely read a possibly-missing key?
explain: A missing key returns the zero value, which is ambiguous. The second return ok tells you if the key exists. Always use comma-ok for lookups that matter.

q: Reading from a nil map vs writing to one?
explain: Read from nil map gives zero value, no panic. Write to nil map panics: assignment to entry in nil map. Always make() or literal-init before writing.

q: What does delete do to a missing key?
explain: delete is forgiving: missing keys are ignored, no error, no panic. Perfect for cleanup loops.

q: Why can this loop be slow on huge data?
explain: Starting from nil, append doubles capacity many times, copying each round. Pre-allocate: out := make([]int, 0, 1000000) for a big speedup.

q: len and cap of a 3-key map?
explain: cap only applies to slices/arrays/channels. For maps just use len(m).

q: What is missing for this to compile?
explain: Unkeyed literals depend on field order and break when fields are added. Prefer User{Name: "Ada", Age: 36}.

q: Pointer or value receiver for SetAge?
explain: Value receivers get a COPY. Mutating methods need pointer receivers. Rule of thumb: if one method needs a pointer, use pointers for all of that type.

q: How do you call Inner.Hello through Outer?
code:
type Outer struct { Inner }
var o Outer
explain: Embedded fields promote their methods to the outer struct. It is composition, not inheritance.

q: How does a type satisfy this interface?
explain: No implements keyword in Go. If your type has the method set, it satisfies the interface automatically. That is why any accepts everything.

q: What does new(User) return?
explain: new(T) allocates a zero T and returns *T. &User{} is nearly identical but allows field initialization.

q: What JSON key does Name produce?
explain: Struct tags control encoding/json. Without the tag you would get "Name". Unexported (lowercase) fields are always ignored.

q: What does go do here?
explain: go launches a goroutine: a cheap concurrent function. The program may exit before it finishes unless you synchronize (WaitGroup/channel).

q: What happens at ch <- 1 with no receiver?
explain: Unbuffered channels are rendezvous points: send blocks until a receiver is ready and vice versa. Buffered channels (make(chan int, N)) allow N sends without blocking.

q: What is select used for?
explain: select multiplexes channels. If several are ready it picks randomly; add default: for non-blocking behavior, and time.After for timeouts.

q: What does this print in old Go (<1.22)?
explain: Before Go 1.22 there was exactly ONE loop variable shared by every iteration, so all goroutines usually printed the final value (3 3 3). Two fixes that work everywhere: pass v as a parameter — go func(v int){...}(v) — or shadow it with v := v inside the loop. Go 1.22+ gives each iteration its own variable.

q: What is missing — what breaks?
explain: The counter starts at 0, and Wait returns the moment it hits 0 — so with no Add, it returns instantly and main exits early. Always Add from the launching goroutine (never inside the new one), or Wait can slip through before any Add lands.

q: How many sends fit without blocking?
explain: Capacity 2 means two values can sit in the buffer. The third send waits for a receiver. len(ch) shows buffered count.

q: How many OS threads can goroutines use?
explain: Goroutines start at ~2KB stacks and are scheduled by the Go runtime. You can run 100k of them; the OS could never do 100k threads.

q: What is the Go error-handling style?
explain: No try/catch in Go. Functions return (value, error) and callers handle it now. Verbose but explicit — you always see the failure path.

q: %v vs %w when wrapping?
explain: %w wraps so errors.Is/As can unwrap through layers. %v only prints. Always %w when callers may need to inspect the cause.

q: In what order do these print?
explain: Defers run last-in-first-out, like plates unstacking: 3 prints first (it is not deferred), then 2, then 1. The twist: each defer’s ARGUMENTS evaluate immediately — defer fmt.Println(x) snapshots x now, even though the call itself waits for return.

q: When is panic appropriate?
explain: panic is for impossible states (nil deref, corrupt init), not bad user input. Libraries should return errors; panics crash unless recovered.

q: How do you compare a wrapped sentinel error?
explain: Never == on wrapped errors. errors.Is walks the chain; errors.As extracts a typed error into a target.

q: What does this return?
explain: With named results, return 41 first assigns n=41, THEN deferred calls run before control truly leaves — and they can still touch n. The deferred closure bumps it to 42. Powerful for cleanup that adjusts results, but confusing enough to use sparingly.

q: Why does decoding skip the secret field?
explain: Only exported (Capitalized) fields marshal. secret stays empty no matter the tags. Same rule for all reflection-based libs.

q: Modern way to check membership?
explain: The slices + maps std packages (Go 1.21) ended the hand-rolled contains helper era. Also: slices.Sort, maps.Keys, …

q: What does ListenAndServe do with nil?
explain: nil means “use DefaultServeMux” where HandleFunc registered. It blocks; real apps configure http.Server with timeouts.

q: Why take ctx as the FIRST param?
explain: context carries deadlines, cancellation and request values. First-param convention keeps it visible. Never store ctx in structs; pass it down.

q: How long is time.Second really?
explain: time.Duration is nanoseconds. Sleep, Since, Until and time.After all build on it. Use time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond) for halves.

q: Fastest way to concat in a loop?
explain: s += x in a loop reallocates every iteration. Builder grows amortized like append. For tiny fixed joins, strings.Join wins.

q: What does //go:embed do?
explain: go:embed ships assets inside one binary — no sidecar files. Embed strings, []byte, or whole dirs as embed.FS.

q: Which files and functions does go test actually run?
explain: go test compiles only files ending in _test.go and runs only funcs starting with Test that take *testing.T. Everything else is ignored.
options: Any file with a test helper

q: What is the idiomatic shape of a table-driven test?
explain: Table tests list cases as data and loop over them. A new case is a new row, not a new function — that is the whole point.

q: What makes this a benchmark instead of a test?
explain: Benchmarks take *testing.B and loop exactly b.N times; the runner scales N until timing stabilizes. Run with go test -bench=.

q: What does go vet catch that the compiler happily allows?
a: Suspicious but legal code, like bad verbs
explain: vet flags likely bugs: wrong Printf verbs, unreachable code, bad struct tags. go test runs a vet subset automatically — run the full thing in CI.
options: Suspicious but legal code, like bad verbs

q: How do you catch data races in your tests?
explain: -race instruments memory access and reports unsynchronized concurrent read/writes with full stacks. Slower runs, but it finds bugs tests alone never will.

q: What does the module line in go.mod actually decide?
a: The import prefix for all its packages
explain: The module path is the import root: package foo inside it imports as example.com/mymod/foo. Versioning and downloads key off this string.
options: The import prefix for all its packages

q: Why call t.Helper() at the top of a test helper?
a: Failures point at the caller, not the helper
explain: t.Helper marks the frame as helper code, so failure lines reference the calling test. Without it, every failure blames the helper body.
options: Failures point at the caller, not the helper
It runs the helper in parallel

q: What does a fuzz test need that a normal test does not?
a: Seed inputs via f.Add plus an f.Fuzz func
explain: Fuzzing needs a seed corpus (f.Add) and the property under test (f.Fuzz). go test -fuzz then mutates inputs hunting for crashes.
options: Seed inputs via f.Add plus an f.Fuzz func

q: What order does ranging over a map produce?
explain: The runtime shuffles map iteration so you can never depend on order. Need order? Collect the keys and sort them yourself.

q: How do you copy slice contents into a fresh array?
explain: copy moves min(len(dst), len(src)) elements and returns how many. Plain assignment only copies the header — both names share one array.

q: How do you branch on the dynamic type inside an interface?
a: A type switch: switch v := i.(type)
explain: The .(type) form is legal only as a switch guard, and each case rebinds v to the concrete type. Nothing else in the language does this.
options: A type switch: switch v := i.(type)

q: Why does this print “not nil”?
a: Interfaces hold type+value; the type is set
explain: An interface is a (type, value) pair and it is nil only when BOTH are unset. Assigning a nil *User fills in the type slot, so i != nil passes while holding nothing. This bites hardest with errors: always return nil explicitly instead of a typed-nil error value.
options: Interfaces hold type+value; the type is set

q: What is the safe way to assert an interface to a type?
explain: The single-value assertion panics on mismatch. Comma-ok reports success in ok instead — the same idiom as map lookups.

q: How do you give a channel receive a deadline?
explain: time.After returns a channel that delivers once. As a select case it races the real work — whichever becomes ready first wins.

q: What does receiving from a closed channel do?
a: Returns zero value at once, ok=false
explain: Receives on a closed channel never block: you get the zero value with ok=false. Sends on closed channels panic — close on the sender side only.
options: Returns zero value at once, ok=false

q: What leaks in this snippet?
a: A goroutine blocked forever on receive
explain: A goroutine parked on a channel nobody will satisfy never exits — a goroutine leak. Every go statement needs a guaranteed exit path.
options: A goroutine blocked forever on receive

q: errors.Is vs errors.As — when do you reach for As?
a: As extracts a typed error; Is only compares
explain: Is asks “is this error in the chain”. As pulls out the first error of a given type so you can read its fields. The target must be a pointer.
options: As extracts a typed error; Is only compares

q: Where is recover() actually able to stop a panic?
explain: recover only catches a panic while a deferred function is running — anywhere else it returns nil and unwinding continues. That is why the pattern is always defer func() { if r := recover(); … }(). Use it at server/goroutine boundaries to log and survive, never as everyday error handling.

q: Why does len("héllo") print 6 instead of 5?
a: len counts bytes; é needs 2 in UTF-8
explain: Strings are byte sequences, so len counts bytes. Use utf8.RuneCountInString for characters, or range over the string, which decodes runes.
options: len counts bytes; é needs 2 in UTF-8

q: What must a type define to satisfy http.Handler?
explain: One method: ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request). HandleFunc adapts ordinary funcs with that exact signature.

q: What does importing a package with _ accomplish?
a: Runs the package init for side effects
explain: Blank imports load a package solely for its init() side effects — like registering pprof handlers — without referencing any identifier.
options: Runs the package init for side effects

q: In what order do these three run?
a: Package vars, then init(), then main()
explain: Dependencies first, then package-level variables, then init() functions, and finally main(). Never rely on order across files — keep init minimal.
options: Package vars, then init(), then main()

q: What concurrency pattern is this?
a: Worker pool: fixed goroutines draining a job channel
explain: A fixed crew of goroutines ranges over one shared channel until it closes. Concurrency stays bounded without tracking every goroutine — close jobs when done so workers exit.
options: Worker pool: fixed goroutines draining a job channel

q: What concurrency pattern is this?
explain: Each stage reads a channel, transforms each value, and writes the next channel. Close each out-channel when finished so the downstream range loop can terminate.

q: What concurrency pattern does this goroutine implement?
explain: Fan-in multiplexes several inputs onto a single channel so one loop can consume them all. Its mirror image, fan-out, splits one input across many workers.

q: What does cap() report for a plain array?
explain: Arrays are values with fixed size baked in, so len and cap always agree. Slice one and cap starts telling the truth about headroom.

q: Why does this refuse to compile?
a: := demands at least one NEW variable
explain: Short declaration must declare something new on the left. The second line declares nothing, so the compiler sulks. Plain x = 2 is what you wanted.
options: := demands at least one NEW variable

q: What type is this single-quoted character?
a: int32 — a rune, not a string
explain: Single quotes mean rune (alias int32): one Unicode code point as a number. Double quotes would make it a string. Mix them up and Printf will tell on you.
options: int32 — a rune, not a string

q: How do Go programmers swap two variables?
a: a, b = b, a — parallel assignment
explain: Both sides evaluate first, then assign simultaneously. No temp variable, no cleverness required. It works for function returns too.
options: a, b = b, a — parallel assignment

q: What does ...int collect?
a: A []int slice of all trailing args
explain: Variadic params arrive as one slice. Callers pass values comma-separated, or spread an existing slice with Sum(s...).
options: A []int slice of all trailing args

q: Where does n live after this if?
a: Nowhere — scoped to the if statement
explain: Short declarations in the if initializer die with the statement. Need n later? Declare it before the if and assign with plain =.
options: Nowhere — scoped to the if statement

q: What does bare return hand back here?
a: The named values exactly as they stand
explain: Bare return ships the current named results: n=7, err=nil. Convenient, but readers must hunt for where names were set — use sparingly.
options: The named values exactly as they stand

q: Is goto legal Go?
a: Yes — but it cannot jump over declarations
explain: goto exists and works, with one guardrail: no jumping over new variable declarations. Legal does not mean wise — reach for it almost never.
options: Yes — but it cannot jump over declarations

q: When does a case fall into the next one?
code:
switch n {
case 1:
	fmt.Println("one")
	fallthrough
case 2:
	fmt.Println("two")
}
explain: Go cases break automatically — the opposite of C. fallthrough forces entry into the next case body (without re-checking its condition). Rarely what you want.

q: Why does the const version compile?
code:
const c = 2.5
var f float64 = c
explain: Untyped constants live in a perfect-precision limbo until used, then become whatever the context needs. Typed equivalents lock in early and complain.

q: What does the third index in s[1:2:3] control?
a: Capacity — it caps how far t can grow
explain: Full slice expressions set len AND cap: t has len 1 but can only grow to index 3 of the shared array. It stops append from stomping your neighbors.
options: Capacity — it caps how far t can grow

q: Does append work on a nil slice?
explain: Nil slices have len 0 but append handles allocation for you. This is why var s []int followed by append in a loop is idiomatic Go.

q: Which of these maps can you write to right now?
a: a and b — c is nil and will panic
explain: Literal and make both initialize. var only declares, leaving a nil map that reads fine but panics on write. The compiler will not save you here.
options: a and b — c is nil and will panic

q: How do you zero a slice but keep its length?
explain: clear() (Go 1.21+) zeroes every element in place — length unchanged, backing array kept. On maps it deletes all keys instead.

q: Builtin min and max since Go 1.21?
a: Yes — min and max are builtins now
explain: No more if-else ladders for two values. min/max take any ordered args (even mixed numeric types) and just work.
options: Yes — min and max are builtins now

q: How do you compare two maps?
explain: Maps are only comparable to nil, so == between two maps does not compile. maps.Equal walks both (values must be comparable too).

q: A pointer to the first 4 as a fixed array?
a: Convert — panics if len drops below 4
explain: Slices convert to array pointers when long enough, sharing memory both ways. Shorter than 4 and it panics at runtime. Sharp tool, real edge.
options: Convert — panics if len drops below 4

q: When is an anonymous struct the right call?
explain: Need a shape exactly once — for a test, a JSON blob, a channel message? Skip the type declaration. If it shows up twice, name it.

q: Can this type have methods?
a: Yes — any named type in your package
explain: Methods are not struct-exclusive. Any named type you declare can carry methods. You just cannot add methods to types from other packages.
options: Yes — any named type in your package

q: Which Hello wins when you call b.Hello()?
a: B — the outer method shadows the promoted one
explain: Promoted methods are the fallback, not the override. Anything defined directly on the outer type wins. Embedding is composition with a polite default.
options: B — the outer method shadows the promoted one

q: Why does == work on these structs?
code:
type P struct{ X, Y int }
fmt.Println(P{1,2} == P{1,2})
a: All fields comparable — so is the struct
explain: Struct comparability is inherited: all-comparable fields means comparable struct. Smuggle in one slice or map and == stops compiling.
options: All fields comparable — so is the struct

q: What is User.Greet with no instance?
a: Method expression — receiver becomes first arg
explain: T.Method rebinds the receiver as an explicit first parameter. Its twin, u.Greet, is a method value with the receiver already bound.
options: Method expression — receiver becomes first arg

q: What costs zero bytes and signals presence?
explain: The empty struct occupies zero bytes, so map[string]struct{} is the idiomatic set: keys carry meaning, values cost nothing.

q: Why is this 16 bytes instead of 9?
a: Alignment pads bool to 8 — reorder to shrink
explain: Fields align to their size: the bool eats 1 byte then 7 padding so int64 lands aligned. Biggest fields first keeps structs tight.
options: Alignment pads bool to 8 — reorder to shrink

q: What does chan<- int promise as a parameter?
explain: Channel directions are compile-time contracts. Hand a bidirectional channel to a send-only param and the function physically cannot receive. Self-documenting APIs.

q: When does this loop finally exit?
a: When ch is closed and drained
explain: Ranging over a channel parks until close. Forget to close and the loop (and its goroutine) lives forever — the classic leak. Close on the sender side.
options: When ch is closed and drained

q: What happens at the second Lock()?
explain: Go mutexes have no owner concept and no re-entry. Lock twice from one goroutine and you wait on yourself forever while the runtime judges you.

q: How do you do something every second until told to stop?
explain: Tickers beat steadily until stopped; forgetting Stop leaks the ticker. time.After is for one-shots, Ticker is for rhythms.

q: How do you guarantee setup runs exactly once?
explain: Once.Do runs the function a single time no matter how many goroutines race it. Late callers block, then return immediately. Init logic loves it.

q: What is sync.Pool for?
a: Recycling temp objects to cut GC pressure
explain: Pool hands back used objects instead of allocating. No guarantees — the runtime may drop everything under pressure. Throughput trick, not storage.
options: Recycling temp objects to cut GC pressure

q: Counter without a mutex?
explain: Atomics make one indivisible step: add, load, store, swap. Anything fancier (check-then-act) still needs a mutex. Fast lane, narrow road.

q: WaitGroup that returns errors?
a: errgroup — first error wins, rest cancel
explain: From x/sync: fan out like WaitGroup, but Wait hands back the first error and cancels the shared context. Concurrency with accountability.
options: errgroup — first error wins, rest cancel

q: When do you reach for fmt.Errorf instead of errors.New?
a: To add context and wrap with %w
explain: errors.New makes flat messages. Errorf with %w layers context while keeping the original unwrappable for errors.Is and As. Context is kindness to future-you.
options: To add context and wrap with %w

q: What does log.Fatal do after printing?
a: Calls os.Exit(1) — deferred calls never run
explain: log.Fatal is print-plus-exit, and exit means your defers (file closes! unlocks!) never fire. Fun at 3am. Prefer returning the error; save Fatal for main().
options: Calls os.Exit(1) — deferred calls never run

q: What happens when this Parse fails?
a: It panics — strictly for init-time setup
explain: Must converts check-this-error into crash-if-broken. Perfect for templates and regexes baked in at startup that must be valid; poison anywhere user input flows.
options: It panics — strictly for init-time setup

q: How do you return two errors as one?
a: errors.Join — Is and As see through all of them
explain: Join (Go 1.20+) wraps a list while keeping every member inspectable: errors.Is/As walk the whole tree. Multierror handling without a library.
options: errors.Join — Is and As see through all of them

q: What makes MyErr work with errors.As?
a: An Error() string method on it
explain: Implement error by defining Error() string — that single method is the entire contract. Pointer receivers let As fish out the concrete type.
options: An Error() string method on it

q: Must a panic carry an error?
a: No — any value flies, recover catches all
explain: panic accepts strings, ints, structs, whatever. Convention says errors, but the runtime does not check. recover gets back exactly what you threw.
options: No — any value flies, recover catches all

q: How do you sort these ints biggest-first, modern style?
a: Sort ascending, then Reverse — both in slices
explain: The slices package ended hand-rolled sort code. Sort, then Reverse for descending. For custom order there is SortFunc with a comparator.
options: Sort ascending, then Reverse — both in slices

q: How do you read $HOME and know if it was even set?
explain: os.Getenv hides the difference between empty and unset. LookupEnv hands you ok so you can tell blank password from no password configured.

q: How do you split "a   b" on any whitespace run?
a: Fields — splits on whitespace runs, drops empties
explain: Split needs an exact separator; Fields treats any whitespace run as one delimiter and skips empties. The lazy, correct choice for human-typed text.
options: Fields — splits on whitespace runs, drops empties

q: What stops a slow handler hogging a connection?
explain: Read, Write and Idle timeouts bound every phase of a connection. Without them one dripping client can hold a goroutine hostage indefinitely.

q: What does logging middleware look like?
explain: Middleware is handlers all the way down: take one, return one that does something extra. Chain auth, logging and recovery the same way.

q: How do you visit every file under a dir?
a: WalkDir calls your func per entry
explain: WalkDir walks the tree and calls you back per file and dir. Return SkipDir to prune a subtree, any other error to abort the walk.
options: WalkDir calls your func per entry

q: Modern structured logging in stdlib?
explain: slog (Go 1.21+) logs attributes, not just strings: Info, Warn, Error levels plus JSON or text handlers. Printf debugging finally grew up.

q: How do you list every file that needs gofmt?
a: gofmt -l lists the offenders, changes nothing
explain: The -l flag snitches: it lists files whose formatting differs without touching them. Perfect for CI. Drop -l, add -w, and it just fixes everything.
options: gofmt -l lists the offenders, changes nothing

q: What promise does go mod tidy keep?
a: go.mod mirrors actual imports — nothing extra, nothing missing
explain: Tidy scans your code and syncs go.mod and go.sum to reality: adds what you use, drops what you abandoned. Run it before every commit.
options: go.mod mirrors actual imports — nothing extra, nothing missing

q: How do you run only TestAdd, verbosely, everywhere?
a: -run filters by regex, -v narrates each test
explain: -run takes a regex matched against test names. -v streams every PASS and FAIL as it happens. The two flags you will type daily.
options: -run filters by regex, -v narrates each test

q: What does this first line do to the file?
a: Build constraint — compiles on linux only
explain: Build tags include or exclude whole files per OS, arch, or custom tags. Cross-compile for Windows and this file politely vanishes.
options: Build constraint — compiles on linux only

q: What does [T any] buy you here?
a: One function for every element type
explain: Type parameters turn copy-paste overloads into one function. T is decided at each call site — ints today, strings tomorrow, zero runtime cost.
options: One function for every element type

q: Why comparable instead of any here?
explain: any accepts everything, but map keys need == and !=. comparable is the constraint that promises exactly that. Slices can never satisfy it.

q: Do you need First[int](s) spelled out?
a: No — types infer from the arguments
explain: The compiler reads the argument types and fills in T for you. Spell arguments out only when inference stalls, which is rarer than you fear.
options: No — types infer from the arguments

q: What is any, really?
explain: any is exactly interface{} with better marketing: the empty interface accepts every type. Useful, but every any is a type assertion waiting to happen.

q: Where do Ordered and friends live?
a: cmp package — slices and maps build on it too
explain: cmp.Ordered covers every ordered type (< works on all of them). The stdlib slices and maps packages are built on the same constraints you can import.
options: cmp package — slices and maps build on it too

q: Why does this method fail to compile?
a: Methods cannot introduce new type params
explain: A method reuses its receiver type params but may never declare fresh ones. Need Map over U? Write a plain generic function instead — the gods demand it.
options: Methods cannot introduce new type params
Methods cannot be generic at all

q: What can you range over since Go 1.23?
explain: Range-over-func lets you iterate anything a function can yield: filtered streams, tree walks, custom sequences. The function pauses at each yield and resumes after.

q: When can you skip the type arguments?
a: When they infer from the parameters
explain: The scary-looking signature fills itself in from your arguments. Generics read worse than they write.
options: When they infer from the parameters

q: What single method makes something an io.Reader?
a: Read into p, report bytes plus error
explain: One method, entire ecosystem: files, sockets, buffers, gzip streams all speak Read. Return io.EOF when dry — that is the only special error.
options: Read into p, report bytes plus error

q: What does io.Copy return?
a: Bytes copied plus first error — EOF swallowed
explain: Copy streams reader to writer without loading everything. Fewer bytes than expected with nil error just means EOF arrived — totally normal.
options: Bytes copied plus first error — EOF swallowed

q: Decode a stream of JSON values, not one blob?
explain: Unmarshal wants the whole document at once. Decoder pulls values incrementally — perfect for NDJSON logs and endless API streams.

q: Lines without loading the whole file?
a: Scanner buffers and splits for you
explain: Scanner handles chunking and newlines; you just loop. Always check sc.Err() after — I/O errors hide there, not in Scan.
options: Scanner buffers and splits for you

q: How do you print 2026-09-16 15:04?
explain: Go formats by example: Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006 is the magic reference. YYYY-MM-DD prints literally — the classic newcomer trap.

q: String to int, with the error handled?
explain: Atoi is ASCII-to-integer with an error for junk input. Itoa goes the other way. Never parse without handling what failure means.

q: MustCompile versus Compile?
a: Must panics on a bad pattern — globals only
explain: MustCompile is for patterns baked into the program that must be valid — typically package-level vars. User-supplied patterns get Compile plus error handling.
options: Must panics on a bad pattern — globals only

q: Building bytes rather than a string?
explain: strings.Builder outputs strings; bytes.Buffer accumulates bytes and also implements Reader. Pick by what the next consumer eats.

q: What are ExampleXxx functions for?
a: Runnable docs — the output comment is verified
explain: Examples appear in godoc AND run as tests: a mismatched Output comment fails the build. Documentation that cannot rot.
options: Runnable docs — the output comment is verified

q: How do you see which lines tests actually hit?
explain: The profile records every executed block; the HTML viewer paints your code green and red. Chase the red that matters, ignore the rest.

q: How do you read docs offline in a terminal?
a: go doc — stdlib and modules included
explain: go doc prints package and symbol docs right in your terminal, for stdlib and your dependencies alike. Faster than a browser tab.
options: go doc — stdlib and modules included

q: How do multiple local modules share one build?
a: go.work workspace — local modules resolve together
explain: Workspaces let several modules develop side by side with local replaces handled automatically. Commit go.work for team setups, or keep it personal.
options: go.work workspace — local modules resolve together

q: What does append return, and why must you keep it?
a: A new slice header — assign it back
explain: append may grow into a new array; the old header keeps the old length and array. Dropping the return value silently loses the append.
options: A new slice header — assign it back

q: Two slices share one backing array. You sort one. What happens to the other?
a: It changes too — same backing array
explain: Slices are windows, not copies: a and nums look at the same slots. Sorting through one window rearranges what the other sees.
options: It changes too — same backing array

q: make([]int, 0, 3), then appends. Which append reallocates first?
explain: cap 3 books three rooms: the first three appends just move tenants in. The 4th finds no room and Go allocates a bigger array and copies over.

q: Dedup a sorted slice in one pass with no extra memory. What do you need?
explain: One reader marches ahead; a writer index w only advances on new values, copying each first-timer into place. O(n) time, O(1) space — two pointers in disguise.

q: Walking a linked list: when do you stop?
code: for cur := head; cur != nil; cur = cur.Next
a: At nil — the address of nothing
explain: The last box points nowhere (nil). The loop follows Next until there is no next — no counting, no indexes, just arrows to nil.
options: At nil — the address of nothing

q: Which method can rewire the list it is called on?
explain: Value receivers get a copy: rewiring the copy's Next changes nothing. *Node methods edit the real boxes through their addresses.

q: Slow strolls 1 box/round, fast sprints 2. Fast hits nil. Where is slow?
explain: Fast covers twice the ground, so when it runs out of track slow has covered exactly half. One pass, no counting, no length needed.

q: Big-O of a map lookup by key?
explain: Hashing jumps straight to the drawer: four entries or four million cost the same single hop.

q: Binary search demands what before it runs?
explain: Halving only works when 'too small, go right' is always true — that promise is sorted order. Unsorted input makes every guess a lie.

q: for i, r := range "héllo" — what are i and r?
explain: range decodes UTF-8: r is the whole letter (é is one r), i is its byte offset. Byte-thinking breaks on non-ASCII; rune-thinking doesn't.

q: Reading a missing map key returns what?
a: Zero value — no error, no panic
explain: Missing keys read as 0/""/false. The comma-ok form (v, ok := m[k]) is how you tell 'missing' apart from 'really zero'.
options: Zero value — no error, no panic

q: Nested loops comparing every pair of n items cost what?
code:
for _, x := range xs {
	for _, y := range xs {
explain: Every first meets every second: double n, quadruple the work. The classic cure is a map turning the inner scan into a lookup.
options: O(n) — two loops, twice as fast
